utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good morning, everybody. Could the case please be called.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Nicholas Koumjian -- good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian and Ann Sutherland with Ruth Karper, case manager, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Without further ado, let's continue with relevant questions from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no further questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The transcripts of yesterday, last page, read in another way, but sleeping over the night, one can always come to better conclusions, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dr. Cehajic, we have several questions just for clarification, please. The first one is a more general. Yesterday, you were confronted with a long list of names, a list of employees whose employment has been terminated, a list of 113. You can't understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Translator. English [Interpretation] Now I can hear you. A moment ago, I was just hearing English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you understand now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry for this, please. Yesterday, you were confronted with a long list of names, a list of employees whose employment has been terminated, a list of 114 persons. And you identified, I would say probably -- correct me if I am wrong -- by name, by the fact that you know the one or other persons to which nationality, to which ethnicity the persons belong. It is correct that in the past, you had been active in politics. Right?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in an amateur way. Not professionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: During that time, or in the framework of your work for the hospital, have you ever been confronted with a similar list of names of people working, for example, in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the period from the 30th of April, 1992? Was that your question, Your Honour, whether I saw such a list at work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... The former period, before the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not. There was never such a list. There were never such cases of termination of employment, just some individual cases having to do with administrative matters, the expiration of contract or something similar. It was possible for a person to become surplus or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever make such a distinction as you made yesterday, asked by the OTP on the basis of this document whether people is a Croat, Muslim, Serb, Bosniak, or whatever? Did you make such distinctions?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, and I had a feeling that that was the case with other people as well during that period of time. I was not even aware of the percentage of Croats, Serbs, or Muslims working at the hospital. It was not the subject of my interest in any way. It didn't seem to be information that was important in any way. We had normal communication amongst ourselves. I had normal contact with everybody else, and I thought that other people had this normal attitude towards me. I think of that period of time as the best period in my life, best period of my life. I don't think that people were obsessed with the issue of ethnic background at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. But before leaving the list before us, yesterday, on the basis of a question of the OTP, you especially referred to number 111, Zec Dubravka. And I would ask the usher to put Document 65 ter number 625 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make a suggestion or a request, that we mark these exhibits before the witness discusses them. I think when all of us come to the point where we're writing either for our submissions at the end of the case or Your Honour's judgement and we're trying to find where a document is referred to in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I asked you yesterday whether or not you want to tender. You said no, and therefore this document will of course be marked J1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I saw it here for the first time. Never in the past had I seen such a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind and read out this document.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Working organisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Probably it's easier when you have the document before you.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Working organisation, medical centre, Dr. Mladen Stojanovic, Prijedor, OOURRZ, general hospital Prijedor. Number 02-674/3, dated 25th of May, 1992. Pursuant to Article 75, paragraph 2, item 3 on the law on basic employment rights and in connection with the conclusions with the Prijedor municipality Crisis Staff, number 02-111-132/92 of the 5th of June, 1992, I hereby adopt this decision on the termination of employment of Dr. Dubravka, Zec, occupying the post of resident in the organisational unit of biochemical laboratory is hereby terminated as of the 25th of May, 1992, because of unaccused absence during work obligation. All employment rights of the above named shall be discontinued on the date when employment is terminated. Explanation: Due to the general mobilisation that was announced on the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, work obligation has been introduced to the Dr. Mladen Stojanovic medical centre RO in Prijedor. It applies to all employees and has been in effect since the 25th of May, 1992. At its session held on the 5th of June, 1992, the Prijedor Crisis Staff adopted the conclusion whereby all OOUR managing directors shall terminate the employment of all workers who failed to respond to the work obligation. According to Article 75, paragraph 2, item 3 of the law on basic employment rights, termination of employment ensues without consulting the employee if the employee has been absent from work without excuse for five working days. As the above-named employee has not responded to the work obligation within the given period of time, the above-mentioned conditions for the adoption of the decision of the termination of employment have been met. Legal remedy: Employee has the right to appeal to the OOUR workers' council within 15 days of the receipt of this decision. Copies: Above-mentioned, acting OOURRZ managing director, personnel department, claims department, files. Acting OOURRZ managing director, Dr. Radojka Elenkov, internist, internal medicine specialist."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever seen before the signature --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, if I could just make a correction. You referred to the document as P625 when in fact it's P476 of the Rule 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you for this clarification. Have you ever seen before the signature of this person, Dr. Radojka Elenkov?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have, but I don't remember whether this is indeed her signature. She was a colleague of mine. We worked together, but you know doctors' handwritings are sometimes difficult to decipher. I don't exactly remember what her signature looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that this person, Zec Dubravka, was a Croat. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, continue.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- She is a native of Prijedor, and she comes from a local Prijedor family, family that has lived in Prijedor for many years. So I know for sure that she is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss this dismissal with Zec Dubravka or Dr. Elenkov?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I never had an opportunity to discuss this either with Dr. Elenkov or anyone else, because at this time, or at the 25th of May, I was not there. I mean, I would have -- could have signed this document or Dr. Tesinic. I was supposed to sign this document if this, indeed, happened on the 25th of May. It should have been me who signed this document but I never saw this document, nor did I sign it, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Why do you say "it should have been me"?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this was part of my function. The authority to sign such a document was vested with the director. The director at the time was Dr. Tesinic. When he was absent, I had the authority to sign such documents. I would just make a note, "for director," and then sign my name underneath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. To come to another topic, yesterday during the cross-examination, you mentioned more or less spontaneously on page 78, line 7 and following, that you have been on duty the 22nd of May. You said: "I was" -- I quote line 10 -- "I was at the hospital, and I came to the surgery where I was present. I went where some reporters, journalists from Radio Prijedor were shooting on a videocassette conversation with people who were in the vehicle that later took place at the incident in at Hambarine." Here it's quoted. I have this as witness. I quote from the transcript: "Something would happen to me. I was scared that night because I heard what this young man had said -- actually two young men were in the surgery who were slightly hurt, and the third man was also hurt much more. I didn't see him." Did you ever hear anything more about the background of this incident, about the injuries of the three persons?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, no. It was impossible for me to learn about the truth. But the story went around that the three young men -- the three young men had been killed. However, I saw two of them. One of them spoke, and this is what I heard. And I realised that this young man was able to speak normally. He was probably wounded but I didn't examine him or anything, nor did I investigate the -- inquire about the issue. But as I was already in a very uncomfortable situation, I went back. But I was witness to what was -- to the stories that were going around at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know, by chance, when the three persons were able to leave the hospital, or did they ever leave the hospital? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I could no longer inquire about this event. And it happened on the night of the 22nd. The next morning, I left home. It was on the 23rd. Therefore, I was off duty on Saturday and Sunday. I worked on Monday and Tuesday, and on Wednesday at about 10.00, I left the hospital and I never returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again to return to another topic, during the cross-examination, page 33, line 14, you mentioned a document, and you said: "And the document was dated the 18th of August in which it is written that my husband and some other men, some other persons, had been turned to the military court and that he was no longer under the authority of that particular court. This document was signed by..." and then it was not possible to follow. You mentioned a name. Could you please repeat and spell the name of this person. The document was signed by whom, please?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zivko Dragosavljevic, who is a judge, who now lives in Prijedor. I think that he's the president of the local Court there, but he still works as a judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss this issue with this judge later on?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever heard something about a case established against your husband, any kind of indictment or whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. For me, it was impossible to get access to any such documents officially. Nobody officially informed me of anything, so I don't know whether there was any indictment at all. Those were not normal times. In a normal society, persons suspected of having done something wrong must be properly accused, charged with the criminal offence and officially indicted. But those were not, as I said, the normal times, and it was not possible to prove either guilt or innocence. There was nothing that I could do about my husband, and my husband didn't stand any chance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think all persons present in this courtroom know about these problems. You mentioned, in addition, that you have this document, not here but at home. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is a copy of the original document. I was given this by a lawyer who currently resides in Prijedor. He told me that he was supposed to be his lawyer ex officio, and I made contact with him. In August, I kept inquiring about the whereabouts of my husband, and he was the one who told me that he had received the information to the effect that he was no longer there. And he was the one who gave me the copy of this document, and I've kept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please be so kind and provide the Tribunal with a copy of this copy and send it -- I think it's the most appropriate way, if the parties so agree, to the Office of the Prosecutor. Please make the --

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- Necessary arrangements. Thank you. Thank you, these were my additional questions. Then, please, Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Dr. Cehajic, as far as I understand from your statements made in August of 1997 and yesterday, your husband was arrested by the police, and he was detained in the camp, guarded by the military. You were summoned for interrogations by the militaries. Soldiers were put on guard outside your apartment. Soldiers and policemen searched your apartment. Soldiers confiscated your car, and you were advised to request an official confirmation about the confiscation from the military barracks in Urije. Nevertheless, after the arrest and detention of your husband, you, for several times, tried to reach Dr. Kovacevic and Dr. Stakic, and not the police chief or military command. Why? Can you explain it?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mayor was the person in that town who was supposed to care about each of the citizens. That was the first explanation, and I thought they had worked together. And the third was that he ought to know what had happened with his predecessor. And also, they took over the authority, and the person who had authority also was in charge of the police and of the military. So it was all connected, who was giving orders and who was listening to -- obeying the orders. So it was a community which had to function in such a way, because it was not possible that it functioned differently. I thought that they had the authority, and that's why I thought that they would be able to help me. This was my initial idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what do you think why all your attempts to reach Dr. Stakic and Mr. Kovacevic failed?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was arranged in such a way and that it wasn't possible for me to achieve anything. Even if I had gotten to -- reached him, they wouldn't have helped me, so it was better to prevent someone to come to you. This is how I think. Maybe that was not the case. Maybe Dr. Stakic doesn't even know that I looked for him and wanted to see him. But this could have been the arrangement that -- for everyone as well as for me that they didn't want to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that Dr. Stakic denied the existence of the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was surprised at that moment, even while I was in the shock because of the war. But I'm not any more because of you have to use all the mechanisms to be able to live normally, and I thought "how is it possible that he says to people that it didn't exist"? Not others, not non-Serbs, but his people knew that there was the Omarska camp, and that he knew and they knew. So now he said that there was no Omarska camp. So at that point, that was the only possible way how to explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: You were interrogated in Prijedor army barracks and in Keraterm camp. Who were the interrogators? Were they military or civilian or paramilitary or policemen?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the barracks, I said that they actually took me in. Nobody interrogated me there. The person who took me to the -- for the interrogation, he just brought me there, and he took me among all those soldiers, and then he took me back to the car and drove me to the Keraterm premises where a man who was a civilian interrogated me. He was a civilian. And there was no uniform. He was not wearing uniform or any signs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I have no more questions. [No Interpretation] Dr. Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we finally conclude, I think this important part of your life would not be complete without touching upon a decision on the termination of employment. Could the usher please put this document first on the ELMO, that we all can see what it's about, and then I would ask you to read out this document. This was 65 ter Document Number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: 625. And we have an extra copy if Your Honour would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's fine. 625. And we treat it from now on as J2.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The medical centre, Dr. Mladen Stojanovic in Prijedor. Number 02804/135. Date: The 7th of October, 1992. Pursuant to Article 75, the statute item 3 of the law on the basic rights of employment in the SFRY, and Article 125, paragraph 2 of the rules on employment in the Prijedor general hospital basic organisation of associated labour, the acting director issues the following decision: On termination of employment: This is to confirm that the employment of Dr. Minka Cehajic in the Prijedor general hospital ended on the 18 September, 1992." It is probably September the 18th, 1992. "Due to an unjustified absence from work of five consecutive working days. "Reasons: Following a public announcement in the Kozarski Vjesnik on the 11th of September, 1992, all workers who were put on standby were to report at work on the 18th of September, 1992 in order to be registered. The above-mentioned employee failed to report for work on the given date, thereby fulfilling the legal conditions for termination of employment on the basis of an unjustified absence from work of five working days -- consecutive working days pursuant to Article 75, paragraph 1, item 3 of the law on the basic rights of employment in the SFRY. "Based on these reasons, it was decided as in the above decision. "Legal remedy: Worker who is not satisfied with this decision has the right to appeal to the administration board of the work organisation within 15 days of the day of receipt. "The acting director, the above-named, claims office, personnel, files, and the director who signed, acting director, Ranko Sikman, health organisation engineer."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dr. Cehajic, when did you receive this document?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never received this document. This is the first time that I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please finally --

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. My workbook, I was looking for it two years ago in Prijedor. I do go to Prijedor, but at that time I didn't go very often, and I asked some people that an employee gave me. So they did give me my workbook in which it is written that my employment ceased to exist on the 1st of September, 1992. And here, it says that it was much later. So this is the only thing that I have in my workbook on the termination of my employment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Someone later meet this Ranko Sikman who signed this document before you?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had known him before that, because he used to work in the laboratory. And I know that he became the director of the work organisation of the medical centre Dr. Mladen Stojanovic at that time. But ever since, I have not seen him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Cehajic, do you have J1 in front of you, the document in relation to Dr. Dubravka, Zec?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That document states that the person that's referred to in that document, their work will be terminated because they haven't responded to the work obligation. Do you know whether Dr. Zec was at work during the end of May, the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just remembered that she was, but I only think because of what is written here that she at that time was not in the laboratory in Prijedor, that she was on specialisation. Where could she have been? In Belgrade, Zagreb, or Sarajevo at that time, because that was the way of education. We were a general hospital in which if anybody had to have some additional education, they had to go to a larger institution in order to do that. I went. Everybody else went. And I suppose that at that time, she was there. And this was the working period. She was paid during that time, but she was only -- I suppose she was in Zagreb at the hospital, maybe even in Belgrade. She worked there, and she was paid for that every month.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do have a couple.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, good morning again. With respect to exhibit J1 that you have in front of you, under paragraph number 1, under decisions, it actually has the word "radno mjesto" which identifies the workplace of this particular doctor. Correct? Second line under paragraph number 1.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, if the doctor that is mentioned here in this exhibit J1 would have been working in the Prijedor hospital, they would have listed that as the place of employment for the doctor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was employed with the hospital. And if at that time she was on specialisation, she could have been somewhere in the clinic in Zagreb or elsewhere. But I don't know how many people worked on that particular day, because this was the registration. And each unit had a control of who was on leave or who was working at that time. It was not my duty. It was the duty of the people who were in charge of that particular unit or laboratory. But this reminds me that maybe she was at that time on specialisation, and she could have been absent because she was in Zagreb, Belgrade, or Sarajevo at a clinic. And that on the 25th or the 5th of May -- of June, that she could not be at the hospital in Prijedor. I'm only saying that that is a possibility because that was not a question. But for some people who were on specialisation, I saw that their employment was terminated with no reason whatsoever because they had had an agreement, a contract, with a hospital that they would be receiving their salary and that they would spend at some institution for specialisation some time, but they would still be paid. So all the costs would be borne by the unit of the hospital. I suppose, because this is written here that she was on specialisation, that she started working, and she hadn't completed her specialisation. But I did see for some people who were on specialisation then that they -- their contract of employment was terminated because they were not there. They couldn't have been there because they were on specialisation. I don't know under which number, but Hodzic Nermina, I'm sure that she was in Tuzla on specialisation, but she had her contract. When this happened, there was no reason for her employment to be terminated, because she could not respond because she had been on education at a different institution elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, are you familiar with any Serbs, in particular referencing Exhibit S49B which also were under contract and did not return or respond to the request by the hospital, the local hospital, to return to work who were ultimately discharged or put on leave? Are you familiar with any such cases?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know because I didn't have any documentation because I didn't know what was true and what wasn't. I said that on the 27th I still worked. If some things could have happened then, but they could have been hidden from me. But I thought that the 27th of May, I was supposed to have been informed about everything that was important at the hospital. But there could have been a document that I didn't know of. I only saw people who told me that they had been discharged, and there was all I could know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was there a policy or provision in the hospital that you're aware of at the time when you were a director where the head of the facility would be able to request those physicians or employees who were under contract for specialisation in other areas to return to the hospital in Prijedor on an as-needed basis? Did something like that exist?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such decision, but it was possible that we had such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you're just not aware of it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with Dr. Risto Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Risto Stojanovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with him? And just for the record, if I may interrupt, Doctor --

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know of him. He was a surgeon in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's listed, for the record, as number 19 on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Bench is aware. The witness touched upon this person already yesterday telling us that this is a Serb from Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just wanted the record to be clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know the reasons for the discharge of Dr. Risto Stojanovski?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. But when I worked, I did know that we always discussed that he was supposed to retire. He was an old man. When I came there as a doctor, he was already a specialist. I don't know how old he was. But he was not supposed to work any longer. Within that context, I know that we were preparing him to retire because a surgeon cannot work being very old. He did operate, but he could not work a lot, being a surgeon. But how he was discharged, I do not know. If he did receive it, there was a possibility that it was not necessary or it was not possible for him to continue working any longer. But I do believe that he didn't receive it because he was a Macedonian or of orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Dr. Vikalo?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the name. Maybe if I saw him, I would recognise him. What he is, where he is, how he is, I maybe have heard that maybe he is working in Prijedor now, but I cannot talk about it because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have any understanding whether he is a Serb, Bosniak, or Croat?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe because of the name, we could connect him with some ethnicity, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know when or if he was discharged and why?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I saw somewhere that it was written, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about Slavica Nukic? Do you know if she was Serbian, Bosniak, or Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She does work with him, even now. I know that she is a Serb, and that she is married to a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour. Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Reference was made once again to the list of this 114 people where the employment has been terminated between 1st May and 1st July, with a clear emphasis of 25 May, 1992. Can you tell us how many employees had there been at the end of May 1992 in total in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not know the precise number. But I did think, so at some moment we had 550 or 570 employees and sometimes we did employ even more when we needed them. I think when I was there, we had 550 but I cannot be sure hundred per cent. How many there were later on, I would not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I cannot identify any more questions. Then I --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just offer J1 A and B and J2 A and B into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we do this during the change. We'll come back to these administrative matters. But first of all, Dr. Cehajic, thank you very, very much for giving us this insight about that what happened from your point of view. And I know it is difficult to be a witness here, but you can be sure that you gave a contribution for all of us to come closer to the truth. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, Judges, that have made it possible for me to do it. I also would like to ask you, of course, to take this into consideration in a real way and an unbiased way, to judge to what extent who was contributed to what extent to what had happened. Who is not guilty should be freed, and who is guilty must suffer the consequences of what he had done. I do not consider anyone guilty, and I do hope that whoever is not guilty ought to show to this honourable court that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we turn to the next witness, which is a protected witness, I think, the necessary technician -- technical equipment may be arranged. In the meantime, let's take this time. There were two new exhibits, J1A, the English version, and B, the B/C/S version. And J2A and B. Any objections from the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just again for the record, on J1, we object for a number of reasons based on the witness's testimony, she doesn't recognise the document as being the authentic signature of the person who it purports to be. Secondly, we see two or at least two inconsistencies with the date. Purportedly the document was signed and issued, according to the top left hand corner on the 25th of May, 1992; yet the body in reference of the document itself mentioned, relies on, and uses as authority purportedly something that was in existence on the 5th of June, approximately a week or two later, of 1992. That's identified in the first full paragraph of Document J1. Similarly, that date appears on the paragraph in the middle of the -- this document under the "decisions." And it's under Item Number 2, the paragraph following that. Again, it references the date of the discharge, but then also references as reliance upon an authority, something that existed subsequent to the date of the actual discharge. Those would be our objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Bench appreciates your observations, but under the guidelines distributed the 25th of February, 2002, the documents are admitted into evidence under the number J1A, B, and J2A, B. The next witness is ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just that you all know, we have to make a break at 10.25 sharp. There is another initial appearance for me in another courtroom. And then I would ask you to be back again at 11.15. I hope to be back at that point in time. And in return, we continue today until 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We have Mr. Waidyaratne in the on-deck circle to use American baseball terminology, and if Ms. Sutherland can be excused, he will be leading the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The witness needs pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, this witness is closed session with pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it correct, registry, that this witness is Witness E?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. This would be Witness O.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Why O?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Because we have a number of 92 bis witnesses that were assigned pseudonyms. So to follow the order, we resume at O now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification for all of us. I don't know. Do we all have a list of the pseudonyms assigned to 92 bis witnesses? Therefore my surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do not yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But there were no objections to proceed in the way as suggested by the registry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then we know how to call the witness. Thank you for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 1.38 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of May, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
